package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed via multiple vectors, not a package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: Fickle Stealer is a modular, Rust-based infostealer distributed through various attack vectors, including malicious documents, PowerShell scripts, and packed executables. It is designed to steal credentials and sensitive data from browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and applications, exfiltrate files, evade analysis, and self-delete to avoid detection. Its use of privilege escalation, anti-analysis, and propagation techniques makes it a significant threat.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Drops a copy of WmiMgmt.msc and a fake WmiMgmt.msc to C:\Windows\System32 and C:\Windows\System32\en-US, abuses ActiveX to open a web browser, sets up an HttpListener, configures exclusions for the stealer, and downloads/executes the stealer with elevated privileges.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At postinstall/runtime (initial infection), the script drops fake system files (WmiMgmt.msc), abuses ActiveX and HttpListener to open a browser and set up a local web server, configures malware exclusions, and downloads and executes the stealer with elevated privileges, resulting in privilege escalation and initial payload deployment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script performs UAC bypass, drops fake system files, abuses ActiveX and local web servers for privilege escalation, and executes untrusted code with elevated privileges—behaviors strongly associated with malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts should not bypass UAC, drop fake system files, or execute arbitrary binaries with elevated privileges without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IT automation tools may use UAC bypass for legitimate software deployment, but not by dropping fake system files or abusing web server mechanisms.
key_indicators: Dropping fake WmiMgmt.msc in system directories
ActiveX and HttpListener abuse for privilege escalation
Downloading and executing payloads with elevated privileges

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Creates a new scheduled task to execute engine.ps1 after 15 minutes.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (persistence), the script creates a scheduled task to execute engine.ps1 after a 15-minute delay, establishing persistence and enabling delayed execution of the next-stage payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware frequently uses scheduled tasks to maintain persistence and delay execution, making detection and remediation more difficult.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers rarely create hidden scheduled tasks to run additional scripts after a delay, especially without user notification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise software may use scheduled tasks for updates, but not for hidden or delayed execution of unknown scripts.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Enumerates .exe files in user directories (C:\Users\, D:\, E:\, F:\), runs inject.ps1 to inject shellcode that executes u.ps1 from the internet, and logs injected file paths (base64-encoded) to C:\Users\Public\prepares.dat.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (lateral movement/infection), the script enumerates executable files in user directories, uses inject.ps1 to inject shellcode that re-executes the initial payload from the internet, and logs the paths of infected files in base64 format to prepares.dat, resulting in propagation and infection tracking.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Injecting shellcode into executables and maintaining an infection log are classic malware propagation and tracking techniques.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts do not inject code into unrelated executables or keep logs of infected files in hidden locations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may enumerate executables, but do not inject shellcode or maintain covert infection logs.
key_indicators: Enumeration of .exe files in user directories

execution_context.file_location: tgmes.ps1 (PowerShell script, dropped to Temp with random name)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Sends victim information (country, city, IP, OS version, computer/user name) and status messages to attacker's Telegram bot, then deletes itself.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (C2 communication), the script collects system and victim information, sends it to a remote Telegram bot, and deletes itself, resulting in exfiltration of metadata and anti-forensics.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating system information to a Telegram bot and immediate self-deletion are strong indicators of command-and-control and anti-forensics behavior.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts do not send sensitive system information to external messaging platforms or self-delete after execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate monitoring tools may report system info to a central server, but not via Telegram bots or with self-deletion.
key_indicators: Exfiltration of system and user metadata

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Packer replaces the __cinit function in a legitimate executable to allocate memory, decrypt, and execute the stealer payload in memory before WinMain.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (payload unpacking), the packer modifies the __cinit function of a legitimate executable to allocate memory, decrypt the stealer payload, and execute it in memory before the main application logic runs, resulting in stealthy payload delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Executing code before WinMain and unpacking payloads in memory are advanced evasion techniques used to avoid detection by security products.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications do not alter their initialization routines to run hidden or malicious code before main execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some software packers use in-memory unpacking for protection, but not to execute unauthorized payloads in legitimate binaries.
key_indicators: In-memory decryption and execution of payload

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Checks for debuggers (BeingDebugged flag), blacklisted process names, loaded analysis DLLs, virtual machine artifacts, hardware IDs, and suspicious usernames. Exits or shows fake error if analysis detected.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (anti-analysis), the payload inspects the environment for debuggers, blacklisted processes, analysis DLLs, VM artifacts, hardware IDs, and suspicious usernames, and terminates or displays a fake error if analysis is detected, resulting in evasion of security analysis.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Comprehensive anti-analysis checks are a hallmark of sophisticated malware designed to evade detection and hinder analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not terminate or alter behavior in the presence of debuggers or analysis environments.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some DRM or anti-cheat software may check for debuggers, but not with such breadth or intent to evade forensic analysis.
key_indicators: Detection of VM artifacts and hardware IDs

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Collects files and credentials from browsers, wallets, plugins, and applications; parses browser databases for cookies, history, and login data; copies files to Temp, compresses and base64-encodes them, and sends to C2 server. Also takes a screenshot and deletes itself.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (data theft/exfiltration), the payload collects credentials and files from browsers, wallets, plugins, and applications, parses browser databases for sensitive data, copies and compresses files to Temp, base64-encodes them, exfiltrates the data to the C2 server, captures a screenshot, and deletes itself, resulting in comprehensive data theft and anti-forensics.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Mass data theft, credential exfiltration, screenshot capture, and self-deletion are core behaviors of infostealer malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not harvest or exfiltrate user data, nor does it self-delete after execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or sync tools may access user data, but do not exfiltrate it to unknown servers or self-delete.
key_indicators: Credential and file theft from browsers and wallets
Base64 and Deflate encoding for exfiltration

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (self-deletion), the stealer schedules its own deletion using a delayed command line operation, removing its binary from disk and exiting, resulting in anti-forensics and evidence removal.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-deletion is a classic anti-forensics technique used to hinder investigation and remediation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications do not delete their own binaries after execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some uninstallers may remove themselves after completion, but not in the context of data theft or malware activity.
key_indicators: Use of timeout and forced file deletion

attack_chain.action: Initial delivery via malicious document or downloader (VBA macro, link, or executable) downloads and executes u.ps1/bypass.ps1.
u.ps1/bypass.ps1 bypasses UAC, configures exclusions, and downloads/executes the stealer with elevated privileges.
u.ps1 schedules engine.ps1 to run after a delay for persistence.
engine.ps1 enumerates executables, injects shellcode via inject.ps1 to propagate infection, and logs infected files.
tgmes.ps1 exfiltrates victim info and status to Telegram bot, then self-deletes.
Packed executable unpacks and executes the stealer payload in memory before main application logic.
Stealer payload performs anti-analysis checks and terminates if analysis is detected.
Stealer payload collects and exfiltrates sensitive data, takes a screenshot, and deletes itself.

behavioral_signatures: PowerShell scripts that drop or execute fake system files (e.g., WmiMgmt.msc) in system directories
UAC bypass via Mock Trusted Directories or ActiveX/HttpListener abuse
Creation of scheduled tasks for delayed or hidden script execution
Enumeration and shellcode injection into user executables
Outbound connections to Telegram APIs or suspicious C2 servers
In-memory unpacking and execution of payloads before WinMain in modified binaries
Comprehensive anti-analysis checks (debugger, VM, username, hardware ID, analysis DLLs)
Mass file and credential exfiltration from browsers, wallets, and plugins
Self-deletion of scripts and binaries after execution using command line
file_indicators: u.ps1, bypass.ps1, engine.ps1, inject.ps1, tgmes.ps1 in Temp or user directories
Randomly named PowerShell scripts in Temp
Packed executables with modified __cinit or initialization routines
network_indicators: Outbound connections to Telegram bot APIs
Exfiltration of compressed, base64-encoded JSON data
Frequent short-lived connections during data theft
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for PowerShell scripts that drop or execute fake system files, abuse UAC, or create scheduled tasks. Detect enumeration and shellcode injection into user executables, and watch for outbound connections to Telegram or known C2 IPs. Look for mass file access in browser, wallet, and plugin directories, and self-deleting binaries/scripts. Correlate anti-analysis checks and in-memory unpacking with suspicious process trees. Flag compressed, base64-encoded JSON exfiltration patterns.
